1:
The anger astonishes every voice before any explains it. Gill calls Jonah an amazing man, the strangest and most out of the way man for a prophet one shall ever read of, displeased at the very thing all other ministers rejoice in. Clarke has less patience: this hasty prophet was vexed because his prediction was not fulfilled, caring little whether six hundred and twenty thousand persons perished so long as he did not pass for a deceiver, and having lost sight of the condition attached. Ellicott presses the Hebrew, stronger than the English, and notes that the phrase for anger is literally that it burnt to him, the words used of David at the death of Uzziah. He lists the motives proposed, selfish jealousy for his reputation, a patriotism disappointed that his country's great enemy should go unpunished, and an exclusiveness that could not endure divine clemency extended to the heathen, and thinks something of all these may have blended in his mind. Henry finds three faults: Jonah had so little government of himself as to be angry at all; so little reverence of God as to be angry at what God did; and so little affection for men as to be angry at their conversion.

Calvin spends his energy refuting a gentler reading. An older writer had commended the grief and compared it to the apostle's wish to be accursed for his brethren, holding that Jonah mourned not the sparing of the city but the conversion of the Gentiles as a presage of his nation's ruin. Calvin calls the notion extremely frivolous, since God immediately reproved Jonah, and asks what such an apology can avail a prophet whom God has declared to have acted perversely; nor does he see what good it does to cover by invented pretences what plainly cannot be excused.

Whether what follows deserves the name of prayer divides the two sharpest readings here. Gill denies it outright: it is a very different thing from his praying in the fish's belly, a disorderly prayer put up in the hurry of his spirit and the heat of passion, for prayer should be fervent but not like that of a man in a fever; it begins as a prayer and ends with a petition, though an unlawful one, but has nothing of true prayer in it, no celebration of the divine Being, no confession of sin, only quarrelling with God. Calvin asks the same question and answers the other way. The faithful often approach God in a disturbed state of mind, and their prayers are not wholly rejected though not altogether approved; no work of the godly is free of pollution unless purified by a free pardon. Many prayers of the saints are faulty which, tried by the right rule, would deserve rejection, yet God pardons their defects, so that these turbulent prayers keep their title and honour.

On the motive Calvin is more generous, and then more severe. Jonah did not regard himself, he holds, but had joined his ministry to God's glory, so that if his preaching were found false the reproach would recoil on the one who sent him, as though God had spoken dissemblingly, opening now hell and then heaven. Yet this, Calvin says, shows how much good intentions avail with God: the very best intention by our judgment, condemned by God's own mouth; the zeal was inconsiderate because Jonah would be judge himself. Keil and Delitzsch fills in what Jonah does not say, that his word at home had been that God would not destroy Nineveh if its people repented, so that the flight was an attempt to forestall what has now happened. On the request for death he sets it beside the like prayer of Elijah and marks the difference in the reason, since Elijah pleaded that he was no better than his fathers while Jonah pleads only that death is better.
3:
The request for death is judged, but not harshly. Gill thinks it something that in his passion Jonah did not attempt his own life but asked the Lord to take it, though even that he will not justify. Ellicott sets the wish beside the weariness of Elijah and of Moses, and observes, as a contrast of Hebrew with heathen feeling, that none of these men in their loathing of life ever contemplated suicide. Calvin will not have the prayer ascribed to faith, as some do who imagine that Jonah took a flight in his soul to heaven, free of all fear; he does not think the prophet's mind so heroic. The zeal behind it was pious, but the measure sinful, since it is not in our power to quit this world and we ought to remain in it as long as God keeps us in the station where he has placed us; and he sets against him the apostle, who knew death desirable in his own case yet preferred God's will.

The question God asks in reply is variously rendered and weighted. Gill takes it for a mild reproof, since God might have struck him dead at once and instead leaves a question with him; he reports, without approving, a rabbinic rendering that turns it into, is doing good displeasing to thee. Clarke prefers, is anger good for thee, and answers that it is good for no man; one who joins his own passions to the divine threatenings should not be an overseer in God's house, since a surly bishop or a peevish preacher will bring neither glory to God nor good to man. Ellicott weighs the two families of rendering. The received one agrees better with the context, though the marginal one, which follows the Greek, is a very likely rendering of the Hebrew idiom taken by itself; and he suggests that Jonah gave the question the sense that suited his mood, is thine anger just, which might imply the doom was only deferred and he had been too hasty. Probably, he concludes, the Hebrew word kept both its original and its derived meaning and must be rendered well or very according to the context. Calvin uses the reproof generally: nothing is more fallacious than our own balances, and though the whole world absolved Jonah it would avail nothing against the mouth of God. Had he modestly unburdened his griefs into God's bosom it would have been excusable; but anger is past endurance, being, as one says, a short madness that disturbs all the faculties of the soul.

Whether Jonah left the city before or after the forty days is disputed. Clarke holds the verse refers to what had already passed, and with one editor renders that Jonah had gone out and had sat, so that he left when he delivered his message and waited; the verse, he thinks, should be read as a parenthesis or as the opening of the chapter. Gill reports the same rendering, and a Jewish commentator who takes the narrative to return here to what happened before the forty days ended. Ellicott resists it, saying his own reading of the preceding question removes the need for a pluperfect, otherwise required to explain how the prophet still expected the city's destruction after being irritated by the divine clemency. Calvin argues against the pluperfect otherwise: if Jonah went out before the fortieth day, how could he have known the outcome, since no oracle had told him? It was known by the event itself, so he must have gone out afterwards. Henry leaves the chronology alone and marks the temper, that the beginning of strife with God as with man is as the letting forth of waters, so the breach grows wider and should be suppressed at first; he supposes the Ninevites would have entertained the messenger gladly, had he not been too far out of humour.
6:
What the plant was has been argued for centuries. Gill objects to the older renderings that a worm will not touch a gourd and that neither gourd nor ivy rises upright without props, and identifies the Hebrew word with a plant frequent in Egypt from which an oil was made, known to the rabbis as the oil of kik: the ricinus, which rises to the height of an olive tree and carries very large broad leaves like those of vines. Clarke describes it from one naturalist, whose account makes the trunk hollow and the leaves sometimes as broad as the rim of a hat, so that the plant must be of soft substance, since it grows surprisingly fast. Ellicott gives the strongest argument for it, the derivation of the Hebrew name from an Egyptian word and the rabbinical name for the oil; but he quotes a naturalist who leans the other way, to the gourd of the English version, on practical grounds: in Palestine the two names sound almost alike, and the gourd is commonly used to shade arbours, its rapid growth and large leaves fitting it for trellis-work, while it withers as fast as it shoots, so that after a storm its fruit hangs from the leafless tendrils, a type of melancholy desolation.

Calvin turns the question into a story about how disputes over words are conducted. A tumult arose in one congregation when the bishop read out a new rendering that made the plant an ivy; Calvin thinks those who took offence at so trifling a matter thoughtless and foolish, since they ought to have inquired which version was the better. Nor does he spare the great authority who defended the old reading, holding that superstition so possessed him that he would not have the received Old Testament touched at all, on a suspicion that its text might have been falsified, though he allowed the New Testament to be freshly translated. The translator, Calvin adds, was traduced at Rome for the change and answered his accusers in a very severe manner.

Whether the growth was a miracle is left open. Clarke would render the verb as a pluperfect, so that the Lord had prepared the plant, growing there already though not yet in full leaf, and Jonah made it his tent; yet he grants something supernatural in it, since the text says it came up in a night, and allows that in one night it might have expanded its leaves considerably though the plant existed before. He notes that the Chaldee reads it as here last night and withered this night. Ellicott would render the clause not that God made it come up but that it came up, and observes a play of words on the verb for deliver.

The worm draws out providence in small things. Gill remarks that the God who prepared the plant to rise so suddenly almost as soon prepared a worm to destroy it, and insists that God is the Creator of the least as well as the largest, of worms as well as whales, against ancient teachers who set up one maker for ants and worms and another for the heavens; he is surprised that Arnobius, an orthodox father, should have denied such creatures to be God's work and professed ignorance of their Maker. Calvin makes the same point without the controversy: what seemed to happen by chance was directed by the hidden providence of God, and the gnawings even of worms are directed by his counsel, so that neither herb nor tree withers independently of his purpose, as Christ says the sparrows do not fall without the Father. Clarke explains the mechanism, that the root being eaten through, the plant lost its nourishment and withered. Ellicott suggests the worm may be taken collectively, for a swarm of caterpillars. Keil and Delitzsch has God appointing it at dawn to puncture the tree.
8:
The wind is described from experience and etymology. Clarke says the east wind was of itself parching and the sun made it intolerable; such winds are scorching and suffocating in the East, since deserts of burning sand lie that way, and they carry such multitudes of sand particles as to add greatly to the mischief, which he believes the cause of the ophthalmia so prevalent in Egypt and India. Ellicott works from the root, which means silent, and finds what travellers describe as the quiet kind of sirocco, often more overpowering than the boisterous kind; another scholar, he notes, derives the word differently and makes it a rough, stinging wind. Calvin uses the same wind to state a rule. Winds do not rise of themselves or by chance but are stirred up by a divine power; causes may be found in nature why the air is now tranquil and now disturbed, but God's purpose regulates all these intermediate causes, so that nature is not a blind impulse but a law settled by his will. The only difference is that works flowing in the usual course bear the name of nature and are called miracles when he changes their course, while all alike proceed from him.

On the collapse that follows, Ellicott reads closest. He takes the fainting for sunstroke, notes that the wish is literally that Jonah wished his soul to die, and objects to the italics of the English version in the last clause as unnecessary and weakening, the sentence running simply, better my death than my life. He observes what has changed: physical suffering was now added to the prophet's chagrin and, as usual, deepened the moral depression, so that it seemed much worse that the consistency of his teaching should go for nothing now he was uncomfortable. Gill remarks only that the sun was not merely risen but shining out with great force and heat.

The second question God puts is noticed for what it omits. Gill points out that neither the wind nor the sun is mentioned, because the plant would have sheltered him from both had it lasted, and it was for its loss that Jonah was in such a passion; the question is put, he thinks, to draw out the answer and improve the affair to the end it was designed for. Ellicott makes it sharper: Jonah was hurt at the loss of his shade, not sorry for the destruction of the plant, but it is very true to nature that the moment a worthier excuse is suggested he accepts it, without perceiving that in doing so he has prepared the way for his own condemnation; and he turns the lesson on all who would sacrifice the cause of humanity to some professional or theological difficulty. Calvin reads the approach itself as mercy: God had concealed himself for a time but had not forsaken his servant, and often looks on us from behind, so that though we think he has forgotten us he observes how we go on and raises the falling before we perceive he is near; here he did not wait to be sought but anticipated a man seeking his own destruction.

The answer draws from Clarke the broadest conclusion here. Many suppose the gifts of prophecy and of working miracles the highest that can be conferred on a man, and are widely mistaken, since the gifts do not change the heart. Jonah had the gift of prophecy but not the grace that creates the soul anew; this is the love without which, as the apostle says, prophecy and the removing of mountains are but sounding brass. He was a prophet and yet had all his old bad tempers about him in a shameful predominancy, and Balaam was of the same kind, so that God has given prophecy even to graceless men, though many prophets, Clarke grants, were sanctified before their call.
10:
Calvin states the point of the device and raises the obvious objection. God raised the plant suddenly and let it perish to teach Jonah that his conduct towards the Ninevites was very inhuman; but the comparison, he allows, may appear ill suited, since Jonah felt sorry for the plant only as it concerned himself, and if all the gourds of the world had withered he would not have been touched with grief. His answer is that the likeness holds, because God preserves men for the purpose he designed them: Jonah grieved because he was deprived of the shade, and God does not create men in vain, so it is no wonder he wishes them saved. Gill puts the contrast in a line: Jonah would have spared a worthless weed had it lain in his power; what is such a plant to such a city?

The night phrase is taken figuratively. Clarke holds that coming up in a night and perishing in a night are metaphors for speedy growth and decay, and finds the Chaldee reading it so; an older writer, he adds, assigned this plant an extraordinary rapidity of growth in sandy soil, so that in a few days what was a plant becomes a large shrub. Ellicott observes that the original is a forcible idiom impossible to reproduce: it was son of a night and son of a night perished.

Clarke turns the closing question into speech. How much is the city better than the shrub, and there are in it a hundred and twenty thousand persons; these are young and have not offended, since they knew not their right hand from their left, and should God feel less pity for such innocents than a man for a plant withered in a night? And they have now turned from the sins which drew out the threat, and are fasting and lying in sackcloth. He draws the rule that judgment is threatened against the incorrigibly wicked, and that God looks to the broken and contrite spirit.

Who is counted is disputed. Calvin takes the phrase about the right hand and the left of their age, an opinion he says almost universally received; he reports one writer who feared that so many infants would make the city too large and so included the old and middle-aged, taking the words of those never taught in the school of God, who did not understand right from wrong. Calvin calls that too strained, remarking that Nineveh surpassed most of the great cities of his own day, and that Paris alone held more than four hundred thousand souls. Ellicott reckons the same way and gets six hundred thousand from the number of infants. Calvin adds why the figure is given: God shows how paternally he cares for mankind, and records a large number so it may be the more manifest that he will not fulminate inconsiderately against any nation.

The cattle at the end Ellicott most admires. The clause reads at first like an anticlimax and is really, he thinks, the most striking thing in this marvellous book. That a sympathy could exist between Jonah and the plant anticipates by thousands of years a feeling of modern poetry, and the final touch, that even the cattle are a care to God, leaps at once to a truth our own age has been slow to learn; he closes with two verses of English poetry, one on the meanest flower that blows and one on him who prays best because he loves all creatures great and small. Clarke reaches the same place by a shorter road, that the dumb beasts are objects of compassion, spared for the sake of their penitent owners, since the Lord careth for oxen; the great number of them was for the support of the inhabitants, and the Ninevites had probably gathered them in from the open pasture at the approach of danger.
